entries.title: File descriptors
entries.summary: The small integers that identify open files.
entries.description: A file descriptor is a non-negative integer that indexes a per-process table of open files. `0` is standard input, `1` standard output, `2` standard error (`STDIN_FILENO`, `STDOUT_FILENO`, `STDERR_FILENO`). Calls that create a descriptor (`open`, `creat`, `dup`) return the LOWEST unused number (`dup2` lets you choose it). Each `open` of a file creates a new open-file entry with its own read/write position; `dup`/`dup2` create another descriptor for the SAME entry, so the position is shared. When the same file is opened by several descriptors, the kernel counts how many opens it has.

details.name: Failure
details.text: Calls return -1 on error and set `errno`; a valid descriptor is never negative.

entries.title: open and creat
entries.summary: Open or create a file and get a descriptor.
entries.description: Exactly one access mode plus any extra flags joined with `|`. `mode` (the permissions of a new file) is required when `O_CREAT` is used and ignored otherwise; the real permissions are `mode & ~umask`. `creat(path, mode)` is the same as `open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, mode)`. Returns the descriptor or -1.

details.name: O_RDONLY / O_WRONLY / O_RDWR
details.text: read only / write only / read and write

details.name: O_CREAT
details.text: create the file if it does not exist (needs `mode`)

details.name: O_TRUNC
details.text: empty the file if it exists (with write access)

details.name: O_APPEND
details.text: every write goes to the end of the file

details.name: O_EXCL
details.text: with O_CREAT: fail if the file already exists

details.name: mode bits
details.text: `S_IRUSR S_IWUSR S_IXUSR` (owner), `S_IRGRP …` (group), `S_IROTH …` (others), or an octal number such as `0644`

entries.example:
int fd = open("log.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_APPEND, 0644);
if (fd < 0) { perror("log.txt"); return 1; }
mistakes: Forgetting the `mode` argument with O_CREAT (the file gets random permissions).

entries.title: read and write
entries.summary: Raw byte transfers on a descriptor.
entries.syntax:
ssize_t read(int fd, void *buf, size_t count);
ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count);
entries.description: `read` returns the number of bytes read (it may be LESS than `count`), 0 at end of file, or -1 on error. `write` returns the number of bytes written, which can also be less than requested (for example after a signal): check it. Both advance the file position by the amount transferred. Write exactly what you read: `write(out, buf, n)` with `n` the return value of `read`, not `sizeof buf`.
mistakes: Treating a short read as end of file (only 0 means EOF).
Declaring the result as `int` or `size_t`: it must be signed (`ssize_t`) to hold -1.

entries.title: lseek
entries.syntax: off_t lseek(int fd, off_t offset, int whence);
entries.description: `whence` selects the origin: `SEEK_SET` position = offset, `SEEK_CUR` position = current + offset, `SEEK_END` position = file size + offset. Returns the new position (from the start) or -1. `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END)` returns the file size and `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR)` the current position.
entries.example:
off_t size = lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END);
lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_SET);   /* back to the beginning */

entries.title: close
entries.description: Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. The number becomes free and a later `open` or `dup` may reuse it. Processes have a limited number of descriptors: close what you open.

entries.title: dup and dup2
entries.summary: Duplicate a descriptor; the basis of redirection.
entries.syntax:
int dup(int oldfd);
int dup2(int oldfd, int newfd);
entries.description: `dup` returns the lowest unused descriptor as a copy of `oldfd`. `dup2(oldfd, newfd)` makes `newfd` a copy of `oldfd`, closing `newfd` first if it was open (if both are equal it does nothing). The two descriptors share the same open file: the same position, flags and locks. Both return the new descriptor or -1.

details.name: Redirect stdout to a file
details.text: open the file, `dup2(fd, STDOUT_FILENO)`, then `close(fd)`; from then on `printf`/`write` to descriptor 1 go to the file.

mistakes: Expecting `dup` copies to have independent positions (they share one).
Forgetting to flush stdio buffers before redirecting.

entries.title: mkdir, rmdir, getcwd, chdir
entries.description: `mkdir`, `rmdir` and `chdir` return 0 or -1. `getcwd` fills `buf` with the absolute path of the current directory and returns `buf`, or NULL on error (for example `ERANGE` if the buffer is too small). `rmdir` only removes empty directories. A program changes ITS OWN working directory with `chdir`: it cannot change the directory of the shell that started it.
mistakes: Expecting a `chdir` in a program to affect the calling shell.

entries.title: opendir, readdir, closedir
entries.summary: List the entries of a directory.
entries.description: `opendir` returns NULL on error. Each `readdir` returns the next entry or NULL at the end; the name is in `entry->d_name`. The entries come in no particular order and include `.` (the directory) and `..` (its parent); skip them with `strcmp` when you do not want them. The pointer returned by `readdir` is overwritten by the next call: copy the name (`strdup`) if you need it later.
mistakes: Keeping `e->d_name` pointers after the next readdir.

entries.title: errno, strerror, perror
entries.summary: Find out why a call failed.
entries.description: When a system call or library function fails (typically by returning -1 or NULL) it stores a reason code in `errno`. `strerror(errno)` turns it into text; `perror("prefix")` prints `prefix: text` to stderr. `errno` is only meaningful right after a call that reported failure: a successful call may change it. Print errors to `stderr`, not `stdout`.
mistakes: Reading `errno` after a call that succeeded.
Printing errors with `printf`, which mixes them into the normal output.

entries.title: getenv and access
entries.summary: Read environment variables; test file permissions.
entries.syntax:
char *getenv(const char *name);
int access(const char *path, int mode);
entries.description: `getenv` returns a pointer to the value of a variable, or NULL if it is not set. Do not modify that string: copy it first (for example before using `strtok`). `access` checks whether the calling user may `R_OK` (read), `W_OK` (write), `X_OK` (execute) the path, or whether it exists (`F_OK`); it returns 0 if allowed, -1 otherwise.

details.name: PATH
details.text: A list of directories separated by `:`, searched in order when you run a command.

mistakes: Modifying the string returned by getenv.
Using the result without checking for NULL.

entries.title: atoi and strtol
entries.description: `atoi` is simple but gives no way to detect errors (invalid text gives 0). `strtol` sets `*end` to the first unconverted character, so `*end == '\0'` tells you the whole string was a number; check `errno` for overflow.
